lesson.title: Splitting the Cell: How Cytokinesis Finishes Division
lesson.summary: Cytokinesis is the physical division of the cytoplasm into two separate daughter cells, completing the process that mitosis started when it divided the genetic material.
lesson.body:
Mitosis, ending with telophase, divides and distributes a cell's duplicated genetic material into two identical nuclei, but a cell is not actually two cells until its cytoplasm, organelles, and plasma membrane are also divided. That final physical split is cytokinesis, and it typically begins during late anaphase or telophase, overlapping with the last stages of mitosis so that by the time the two new nuclei have fully reformed, the cell itself is already pinching apart.

In animal cells, cytokinesis is carried out by a structure called the contractile ring, a band of actin microfilaments and myosin motor proteins that assembles just beneath the plasma membrane, positioned so that it forms exactly midway between the two sets of separated chromosomes. As the actin and myosin filaments slide past one another, the same basic sliding mechanism microfilaments use elsewhere in the cell, the ring tightens like a drawstring, pulling the membrane inward to create a visible indentation called the cleavage furrow. The furrow deepens until the cell is pinched into two separate daughter cells, each with its own complete set of chromosomes and a roughly equal share of cytoplasm and organelles.

Plant cells face a problem animal cells do not: a rigid cell wall surrounds the plasma membrane and cannot simply be squeezed in half. Instead of a contractile ring, plant cells build a new wall from the inside out. Vesicles budded from the Golgi apparatus, carrying the building blocks of a new cell wall, are guided to the middle of the cell, where they fuse to form a growing structure called the cell plate. The cell plate expands outward until it reaches and fuses with the existing plasma membrane and cell wall, completing two separate compartments each enclosed by its own membrane and wall.

Cytokinesis matters for more than tidiness. If the contractile ring fails to form or the cleavage furrow does not fully close, a cell can end up with two nuclei sharing one cytoplasm, or with double the normal chromosome number packed into a single nucleus. These outcomes are not just laboratory curiosities: cells that skip or botch cytokinesis are a recognized route to the abnormal chromosome numbers seen in some cancers, a connection worth keeping in mind once you reach the chapters on cell cycle checkpoints and cancer biology.
